newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran Guards say Moslems will kill Rushdie.
newsitem.headline: Iran Guards say Moslems will kill Rushdie.

text.p: Moslems across the globe would not rest until they killed British author Salman Rushdie, a statement from Iran's Revolutionary Guards quoted by the daily newspaper Jomhuri Eslami said on Thursday.

The declaration came on the eve of the anniversary of the late Iranian leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's 1989 fatwa, or religious ruling, sentencing Rushdie to death for alleged blasphemy against Islam in his novel "The Satanic Verses".
"Moslems of the world have always considered Salman Rushdie an apostate and shall not rest until Imam Khomeini's order is implemented," the satement said.
It followed an announcement on Wednesday that a religious foundation had increased the bounty on the Indian-born author's head by $500,000 to $2.5 million.
"Rushdie should know that in the end he will be burnt on the fire which he started," the Guards' statement added.
The Revolutionary Guards, formed after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, comprise an estimated 150,000 men in addition to about 500,000 volunteer fighters.
A radical Tehran university student group also urged the government to ignore diplomatic norms and carry out the edict.

"We seriously urge esteemed officials of the sacred Islamic Republic...to disregard international diplomatic norms and take action to implement the revolutionary fatwa," said the student statement quoted by the daily Salam.

Britain called on Iran on Wednesday to denounce the increased bounty. Campaigners against the death sentence urged Europe to break off all talks with Iran except those aimed at ending the threat on Rushdie's life.
Rushdie has been under 24-hour police protection, although he has in the past year been appearing more often in public.
Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani told a Tehran news conference on Wednesday his government had nothing to do with the reward.
Iranian officials say the ruling is a purely religious matter, unrelated to the government. Tehran has said it would not pursue Rushdie but also stresses it cannot withdraw a religious edict.
